miscs.name: Aji Amarillo
miscs.notes: Aji Amarillo (Spanish for ?yellow chile?) is a small, yellow-orange chile grown in the Andes, primarily in Peru. They have been described as the single most-important ingredient in Peruvian cuisine. They are quite hot, but have a really nice, bright, fruity flavour.

miscs.name: Ajowan
miscs.notes: Ajowan seed (also known as carom seed) is native to southern India and is used commonly throughout southern Asia and the Middle East. It smells and tastes a lot like very strong thyme, though slightly more peppery and with a lightly bitter aftertaste. Dry roasting Ajowan or frying it in oil mellows the flavour and brings out a caraway taste.

miscs.name: Aleppo Chiles
miscs.notes: Aleppo chiles (sometimes known as halaby peppers) are named after the region in northern Syria where they grow. They have a moderate heat level and a wonderful, complex, fruity flavour.

miscs.name: Allspice
miscs.notes: Allspice is a ground mixture of baking spices. In reality, allspice is the berry of the pimento bush, grown mostly in Jamaica. It does, however get its name from the fact that it tastes somewhat like a peppery blend of cinnamon, clove and nutmeg. Allspice loses its flavour very quickly when ground, its recommend to buy whole berries and grinding them yourself just before using.

miscs.name: Ancho Chiles
miscs.notes: When a ripe poblano pepper is dried, it becomes an ancho chile. Anchos are quite mild and are used in all kinds of traditional Mexican cooking. Anchos are deep red-brown and have a wonderful, sweet raisiny flavour that provide lots of personality to food without a lot of heat. These are the most commonly used chile in Mexico.

miscs.name: Baking Soda

miscs.name: Basil
miscs.notes: Basil is one of the most commonly used herbs in the world. Basil is mild and has a slight anise flavour.

miscs.name: Bay Leaves
miscs.notes: Stale leaves have no flavour at all, so if your bay leaves have been sitting in the cupboard for a more than a year it?s time to replace them.

miscs.name: Bentonite
miscs.notes: Clay fining agent that removes proteins and haze.

miscs.name: Birch Bark
miscs.notes: Birch Bark, a spice and herb used in beer brewing, adds a unique flavor profile to the final product. With its distinct earthy and slightly sweet taste, Birch Bark influences the taste of beer by imparting subtle notes of wintergreen, mint, and even leather. This natural ingredient is often used for its aromatic qualities and ability to enhance complexity in various beer styles. Apart from adding flavor, Birch Bark has several properties that make it beneficial for brewing. It contains compounds such as betulinic acid and methyl salicylate which contribute to its characteristic aroma and potential health benefits. Additionally, the antimicrobial properties found in Birch Bark can aid in preserving the freshness of beers during fermentation. Typically utilized in craft breweries or homebrewing settings, Birch Bark finds application in different beer styles including stouts/porters, saisons/farmhouse ales, and gruits (herb-infused beers). Its addition can add depth to dark beers like stouts by complementing their roasty flavors with hints of herbal sweetness. In saisons or farmhouse ales where wild yeast strains are frequently employed for fermentation, Birch Bark contributes an intriguing layer of complexity alongside other spices like coriander or black pepper. Gruits benefit from this botanical ingredient as well because it imparts an earthy quality that aligns with their historical use of herbs instead of hops as bittering agents.

miscs.name: Caraway Seeds
miscs.notes: Caraway seeds have a very distinctive taste and aroma that makes many people think immediately of bread. Caraway has a pungent scent and a warm, bitter flavour. It is often used to flavour pumpernickel and rye bread, crackers, sauerkraut, and pork dishes.

miscs.name: Cardamom, Black
miscs.notes: In a way, it's not fair that this spice has to share its name with the sweet and elegant green cardamom. Black cardamom is a totally different spice, and is not nearly as glamourous. Its pods are large and rough, it has an earthy, smoky flavour and it can never be used as a substitute for the more expensive and popular green variety. It does have its place, though. Black cardamom is used to give depth to Indian cooking, and it can be an important ingredient in many curry masalas.

miscs.name: Cardamom, Green
miscs.notes: Green cardamom is an incredibly versatile spice that enhances both sweet and savoury foods.

miscs.name: Cascabel Chiles
miscs.notes: They are brownish-red and quite hard with a moderate heat and a deep, nutty flavour.

miscs.name: Cayenne Pepper
miscs.notes: cayenne pepper is very spicy and adds quick heat to any dish.

miscs.name: Chai
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 3-77 EBC (typical 40) Chai, a blend of spices and herbs commonly used in tea, has found its way into the world of beer brewing. With its distinct flavor profile that includes notes of cinnamon, cardamom, ginger, cloves, and black pepper, Chai brings a warm and spicy complexity to beers. It adds depth and richness to the taste by influencing both the aroma and flavor profiles. Chai is primarily used as an adjunct ingredient during the brewing process to enhance certain styles of beer. Its properties contribute flavors that pair well with malty or robust beer styles such as stouts, porters, brown ales, or even winter warmers. The combination of Chai 's spiciness with these darker beers creates a harmonious balance that often results in a comforting brew ideal for cooler seasons or festive occasions. Chai -infused beers can have varying levels of spice intensity depending on brewers' preferences but they typically offer an inviting warmth with layers of complex flavors from each individual spice component within Chai itself.

miscs.name: Chicory Root

miscs.name: Chili
miscs.notes: Chili, a popular spice and herb, has found its way into the world of beer brewing, adding a unique twist to traditional brews. Known for its fiery heat and distinct flavor profile, Chili brings intense spiciness and subtle smokiness to beers. Its influence on taste can vary depending on the quantity used - from providing just a hint of warmth in lighter styles to delivering an explosive kick in stronger ones. The addition of Chili to beer is primarily used for enhancing flavors and creating new sensory experiences. It adds complexity by introducing spicy notes that complement or contrast with other ingredients like hops or malt sweetness. Chili 's properties go beyond just heat; it also contributes aromas such as earthy undertones or fruity characteristics when added during fermentation. This versatile ingredient finds its place in various beer styles, including stouts, IPAs ( India Pale Ales ), lagers, and even sour beers – each offering a different balance between heat and flavor intensity.

miscs.name: Chipotle Pepper
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 4-47 EBC (typical 47) Chipotle Pepper, a smoked and dried jalapeño pepper, has found its way into the world of beer brewing to add an intriguing twist to traditional brews. Known for its smoky flavor profile with hints of earthiness and spiciness, Chipotle Pepper brings a unique aroma and taste that can elevate any beer recipe. When used in moderation, it imparts a subtle smokiness that harmonizes well with various malt flavors. The addition of Chipotle Pepper greatly influences the taste of beer by adding complexity and depth to the overall flavor profile. It introduces a gentle heat that lingers on the palate without overpowering other ingredients. Brewers often use this ingredient during different stages of the brewing process such as mashing or boiling to extract desired characteristics from it. This spice is commonly used in crafting robust beers like stouts, porters, brown ales, or even Belgian-style saisons where it complements rich chocolatey notes or balances out sweeter malts with its mild spiciness. With their versatile properties, brewers are able to experiment creatively while incorporating Chipotle Peppers into their recipes to create truly unique and flavorful craft beers.

miscs.name: Cinnamon
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 0-252 EBC (typical 7) Cinnamon, a popular spice derived from the bark of certain tree species, has found its way into the world of beer brewing. Known for its warm and sweet flavor profile with hints of spiciness, cinnamon adds depth and complexity to the taste of beer. Its distinct aroma and taste are easily recognizable and can enhance various beer styles. When used in brewing, cinnamon influences the taste of beer by imparting its unique characteristics. It brings a pleasant warmth to the brew while adding subtle notes of sweetness and spice. Cinnamon is often combined with other ingredients like vanilla or nutmeg to create complex flavors that complement different beer styles. Cinnamon is primarily used as an adjunct ingredient in brewing to add additional layers of flavor to beers such as stouts, porters, winter ales, or pumpkin ales. It pairs well with malty beers due to its ability to balance out their richness with its own distinctive taste. The properties of cinnamon make it suitable for both mashing during brewing or added directly during fermentation stages.

miscs.name: Citric Acid
miscs.notes: Citric acid is a mild natural acid found in citrus fruits; it is responsible for the sourness of lemons and limes. In its pure form, citric acid looks pretty much exactly like granulated sugar and acts as a natural preservative and a tart flavouring. It is sometimes used in the making of wine and ice cream, and is widely used in softdrinks, sour candies and other recipes to mimic the flavour of fresh lemon.

Its strong aroma adds complexity to the taste of beer, influencing it with hints of clove and sometimes even a slight sweetness. The use of clove in brewing enhances the overall sensory experience by providing an additional layer of flavor. Cloves are commonly used as an ingredient in various beer styles such as Belgian witbiers, hefeweizens, and certain spiced ales. It is often added during different stages of the brewing process like mashing or boiling to impart its unique flavors into the brew. miscs.name: Cocoa Nibs

miscs.name: Coconut
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 0-134 EBC (typical 15) Coconut is a versatile ingredient that adds a unique flavor profile to beer brewing. Its tropical and nutty taste, along with its creamy texture, can greatly influence the overall taste of the beer. When used in moderation, coconut imparts a subtle sweetness and an exotic aroma that complements various beer styles. Coconut is commonly used for adding depth and complexity to stouts, porters, and brown ales . It enhances the richness of these darker beers by imparting flavors reminiscent of toasted coconut flakes or even coconut milk. Additionally, it can be used in lighter styles such as wheat beers or IPAs to provide a refreshing twist. The properties of coconut make it ideal for brewing due to its high oil content which contributes to both mouthfeel and head retention. Coconut also contains fermentable sugars that add some additional sweetness during fermentation. Moreover, brewers often use shredded coconut or extract derived from coconuts when incorporating this ingredient into their recipes.

miscs.name: Coffee
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 64-871 EBC (typical 439) Coffee has become a popular addition to beer brewing, adding depth and complexity to the flavor profile. Its rich and robust taste brings notes of roasted bitterness, chocolatey sweetness, and even hints of fruitiness. The use of coffee in beer can greatly influence its taste by enhancing malt flavors or balancing out hop bitterness. It provides an earthy undertone that complements various beer styles. Coffee is primarily used as an ingredient during the brewing process, either added directly into the mash or as part of the cold brew extraction method. Its properties include caffeine content which adds a slight kick to the final product while also contributing antioxidants that offer potential health benefits. Coffee -infused beers are commonly found in stouts and porters due to their natural compatibility with dark malts and roasted flavors, but it can also be incorporated into other styles such as brown ales or IPAs for a unique twist on traditional recipes.

miscs.name: Coffee Beans
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 32-269 EBC (typical 202) Coffee Beans are a popular ingredient in beer brewing, adding unique flavors and aromas to the final product. The flavor profile of Coffee Beans can vary greatly depending on factors such as roasting level and origin, but common notes include roasted, chocolatey, nutty, and even fruity undertones. When used in brewing, Coffee Beans infuse their distinct flavors into the beer, creating a rich and complex taste. The properties of Coffee Beans contribute not only to flavor but also aroma in beer brewing. As they are brewed alongside malted grains during fermentation or cold-brewed separately before blending into the base beer, their oils release aromatic compounds that create enticing scents reminiscent of freshly brewed coffee. They add depth and complexity to the malt character while imparting a pleasant bitterness that balances out sweetness. Coffee bean-infused beers often have a smooth mouthfeel with hints of cocoa or dark chocolate that enhance the overall drinking experience. Coffee Beans are primarily used in specialty beers like stouts and porters due to their complementary flavors. These styles typically feature robust malts with roasted characteristics that pair well with the natural bitterness of Coffee Beans . Additionally, some brewers experiment with incorporating coffee into lighter styles such as pale ales or IPAs for added complexity.

miscs.name: Coriander
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 1-19 EBC (typical 1) Coriander, a popular spice and herb, is widely used in beer brewing to add unique flavors and aromas. It has a distinct flavor profile characterized by citrusy notes with hints of lemon and orange zest. When added to the brewing process, coriander can greatly influence the taste of beer by providing a refreshing and zesty character. Due to its versatile nature, coriander is used for various purposes in beer production. It acts as a natural preservative that helps extend the shelf life of beers while also enhancing their overall flavor. Additionally, it contributes to the complexity of certain styles such as Belgian Witbier or German Hefeweizen. The properties of coriander include its ability to balance sweetness with subtle bitterness and provide an aromatic quality that complements other ingredients in the brew. Typical beer styles brewed with coriander include witbiers (Belgian wheat beers), saisons (farmhouse ales), gose (sour German-style beers), and some spiced winter warmers.

Its influence on the taste of beer can range from subtle hints to more pronounced flavors depending on the amount used during brewing. Fennel can be employed for various purposes. It serves as an excellent ingredient for adding complexity and depth to both traditional and experimental brews. Fennel 's properties include being rich in essential oils such as anethole which contributes to its characteristic aroma and flavor. Additionally, it possesses natural preservative qualities that help prolong the shelf life of brewed beers. Typically used in Belgian-style or spiced beers like saisons or witbiers where herbal flavors are appreciated, Fennel adds an intriguing twist by providing hints of licorice alongside other spices present in these styles.

miscs.name: Fennel Seeds

miscs.name: Ginger
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 0-128 EBC (typical 4) Ginger is a versatile spice that has found its way into the world of beer brewing, adding a unique flavor profile and complexity to various brews. With its distinct spicy and slightly sweet taste, Ginger brings a refreshing kick to beers. Its influence on the taste depends on how it's used - whether grated, sliced, or juiced - but generally, it lends a zesty and warming quality to the final product. Ginger is widely used in brewing as both an ingredient during fermentation and as an addition post-fermentation for additional aroma and flavor enhancement. It can be added at different stages of the brewing process to achieve varying intensities of Ginger character in beer. Additionally, Ginger provides natural preservative properties due to its antimicrobial compounds. Ginger pairs well with various beer styles such as wheat beers (e.g., Belgian witbier ), pale ales, IPAs ( India Pale Ales ), stouts, and even sour beers. Whether it's complementing fruity esters in lighter styles or balancing hop bitterness in more robust brews like IPAs or stouts, Ginger adds depth and complexity while maintaining its own distinctive identity within the overall flavor profile of these beers.

miscs.name: Green Tea

Apart from flavor enhancement, Green tea is used for its numerous properties that benefit both brewers and consumers alike. It acts as a natural preservative due to its antibacterial qualities, extending shelf life while maintaining freshness. Additionally, Green tea contains antioxidants that contribute to potential health benefits when consumed in moderation. Typical beer styles brewed with Green tea range from pale ales and wheat beers to experimental or specialty brews like IPA-infused teas. This infusion offers an exciting fusion between two popular beverages – combining the aromas and flavors of hops with the distinct characteristics of Green tea spices & herbs

The delicate yet distinctive fragrance of Jasmine can greatly influence the overall flavor profile by adding a subtle sweetness and aromatic complexity. Brewers use Jasmine primarily as an adjunct ingredient to enhance specific styles or create innovative brews. It is often utilized in lighter beers such as lagers, wheat beers, or pale ales where its floral characteristics complement the crispness and lightness of these styles. Jasmine 's properties include anti-inflammatory and soothing effects on digestion, making it appealing beyond just its flavor contributions.

miscs.name: Juniper
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 0-97 EBC (typical 1) Juniper is a versatile spice that has found its way into the world of beer brewing. Known for its distinct flavor profile, Juniper adds a refreshing and piney taste to beers. Its influence on the taste of beer can range from subtle undertones to bold and dominant flavors, depending on the amount used in the brewing process. In beer brewing, Juniper is primarily used as an ingredient in specialty or seasonal brews. Its properties contribute not only to the flavor but also to the aroma and color of the final product. Juniper 's unique combination of citrusy and herbal notes lends itself well to various styles such as pale ales, saisons, stouts, and even sour beers.

miscs.name: Juniper Berries
miscs.notes: The small, blue-black berries of the juniper bush are best known in the culinary world for flavouring gin, and their smell and flavour brings this to mind immediately. Thier piney taste cuts nicely through strong, rich flavours for a pleasant contrast. The berries are always sold whole, but they are soft and easy to crush in a mortar or with the flat of a knife.

miscs.name: Kieselsol
miscs.notes: Silica fining agent, usually used with chitosan.

miscs.name: Lactic Acid 88%
miscs.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

miscs.name: Lavender
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 5-12 EBC (typical 12) Lavender, a popular spice and herb, has found its way into the world of beer brewing, adding a unique flavor profile to various styles of beer. With its distinct floral aroma and slightly sweet taste, Lavender enhances the overall sensory experience of drinking beer. Its influence on taste can vary depending on how it is used - when added during the brewing process, it imparts delicate hints of Lavender in both the aroma and flavor. Apart from lending an enticing fragrance to beers, Lavender serves multiple purposes in brewing. It acts as a natural preservative due to its antimicrobial properties and can help extend the shelf life of certain brews. Additionally, this aromatic herb is often utilized for its calming effects and potential health benefits such as reducing anxiety or promoting relaxation. Beer styles that incorporate Lavender range from light Belgian witbiers to hoppy American pale ales . The use of Lavender adds complexity to these beers while complementing other ingredients like citrus fruits or spices commonly found in these styles.

miscs.name: Lemon Peel
miscs.notes: Citrus peels contain loads of essential oils that add an unmistakably sharp tartness to foods.

miscs.name: Lime Leaves
miscs.notes: In terms of flavour, lime leaves have a very distinctive citrusy taste, not necessarily limey, and not quite lemony.

miscs.name: Lime Peel
miscs.notes: Citrus peels contain loads of essential oils that add an unmistakably sharp tartness to foods.

miscs.name: Mace
miscs.notes: Mace is possibly the most interesting and unique of all spices. It?s a little-known fact that mace is from the same seed pod that gives us nutmeg. While nutmeg is the inner seed of the pod, mace is the lacy reddish net that surrounds the outside of the shell. During harvest, the mace is removed whole and dried, at which point it is known as a blade. Mace is very similar to nutmeg in flavour and scent, though a little more delicate and sweet. It is also more expensive, since there is so much less of it in each pod.

miscs.name: Magnesium Chloride
miscs.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

miscs.name: Malic Acid
miscs.notes: The main acid in apples; used to raise acidity in cider and wine.

miscs.name: Marash Chiles
miscs.notes: Crushed Marash chiles are very similar to our Aleppo chiles from Syria, but have an even fruitier taste and are ever so slightly less acidic.

miscs.name: Mint
miscs.notes: Also known as: Peppermint Typical color range: 95-259 EBC (typical 95) Mint is a popular herb used in beer brewing, adding a refreshing and aromatic flavor profile to the brew. Its distinctive taste of coolness and sweetness complements various beer styles, enhancing their overall taste experience. Mint influences the taste of beer by imparting its characteristic flavors through essential oils and compounds present in its leaves. In addition to flavor enhancement, Mint is also used for its medicinal properties. It is believed to aid digestion, provide relief from nausea, and promote relaxation. These attributes make it a suitable ingredient for certain types of beers such as herbal or fruit-infused varieties. When using Mint in brewing, brewers can utilize fresh or dried Mint leaves during different stages of the process - including mashing, boiling, fermentation, or conditioning - depending on the desired intensity of flavor. Typical beer styles that incorporate Mint include wheat beers like Belgian Witbier or American Wheat Ale where it adds an invigorating touch to complement citrusy or fruity notes.

miscs.name: Mulato Chiles
miscs.notes: Mulato chiles are very similar to ancho chiles: both are dried poblanos, but it is the darker, riper poblanos that become mulatos. This extra ripeness makes mulato chiles darker and sweeter than anchos, and gives them an earthier flavour.

miscs.name: Nutmeg
miscs.notes: Nutmeg is a versatile spice that finds its application in the world of beer brewing. Known for its warm and earthy flavor profile, Nutmeg adds a unique depth to the taste of beer. Its distinct sweet and slightly spicy notes create a harmonious balance with other ingredients, enhancing the overall complexity of flavors. When used in beer brewing, Nutmeg influences the taste by imparting a subtle yet noticeable hint of warmth and richness. It complements various styles such as stouts, porters, pumpkin beers, and winter warmers exceptionally well. Nutmeg is often added during different stages of brewing – from mashing to boiling or even during fermentation – allowing it to infuse into the beer and fully develop its aromatic properties. Apart from adding flavor, Nutmeg also brings certain beneficial properties to brewed beers. It contains essential oils like myristicin which possess antimicrobial properties that can aid in preserving the freshness of the brews over time. Additionally, Nutmeg has been associated with digestive benefits when consumed in moderation. In conclusion, Nutmeg serves as an intriguing ingredient in beer brewing due to its distinctive flavor profile and potential health benefits. Brewers creatively incorporate this spice into various styles ranging from dark winter brews to autumnal favorites like pumpkin beers for an enhanced sensory experience.

miscs.name: Oak Spirals
miscs.notes: Oak infusion for aging wine, mead and cider.

miscs.name: Orange Peel
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 0-7 EBC (typical 1) Orange peel is a popular ingredient used in beer brewing, known for its distinct flavor profile that adds a refreshing and citrusy twist to the brew. It imparts a bright and zesty aroma with hints of sweetness and bitterness, which can greatly influence the taste of beer. The orange peel is typically added during various stages of brewing, such as during boiling or fermentation, to extract its essential oils and flavors. The use of orange peel in beer brewing serves multiple purposes. Firstly, it acts as a natural flavor enhancer by adding complexity and depth to the overall taste profile. Additionally, it contributes acidity and brightness to balance out maltiness or hop bitterness in certain styles of beers. Orange peel also brings a pleasant visual appeal when used as garnish or added directly into the fermenter. Apart from its flavorful characteristics, orange peels possess unique properties that make them suitable for brewing applications. They contain essential oils rich in limonene compounds that provide intense aromatics while their high sugar content can contribute to both alcohol production during fermentation and residual sweetness in finished beers. Various beer styles benefit from the addition of orange peel including witbiers (Belgian-style wheat beers), Belgian tripels, saisons (farmhouse ale), pale ales, IPAs ( India Pale Ales ), fruit-infused beers like shandies or radlers, among others. In these styles, orange peel helps create an invigorating and vibrant drinking experience by imparting its delightful citric notes throughout each sip.

miscs.name: Pasilla Chiles
miscs.notes: When the long, twisted chilaca chile is dried it is called a pasilla chile, or sometimes a ?pasilla negro.? Pasilla means ?little raisin? and it gets this name from its flavour ? berry and grape with a hint of licorice. Pasilla chiles are long and black.

miscs.name: Pectic Enzyme
miscs.notes: Breaks down fruit pectin for clearer wine, cider and fruit mead.

miscs.name: Peppercorns, Black
miscs.notes: They are picked when they are green and unripe, and are sun-dried, a process which ferments the berry and turns it hard and black.

miscs.name: Peppercorns, Green
miscs.notes: Green peppercorns are the same as black peppercorns, in that they are picked when green and unripe. But instead of being dried in the sun, they are quickly dehydrated so that they retain their bright green colour and mildly spicy flavour.

miscs.name: Peppercorns, Pink
miscs.notes: Pink peppercorns are not related to actual peppercorns. They are the fruit of the Brazilian pepper tree and are grown in South America. These pink berries are soft and delicate with a papery, brittle shell. They have a fruity flavour that is slightly resinous, similar to juniper berries.

miscs.name: Peppercorns, Szechuan
miscs.notes: Szechuan pepper is the outer husk of the fruit of the Chinese prickly ash tree. The berries are dried and split open, and the bitter seeds inside are discarded. The flavour of Szechuan pepper is very fragrant, lemony and pungent and it has a biting astringency on the tongue

miscs.name: Peppercorns, White
miscs.notes: White peppercorns are picked from the vine when they are almost ripe - much later than black or green peppercorns. When picked, they are a yellowish-pink colour. The peppercorns are treated with water to remove the skin, and then sun-dried. White peppercorns contain less essential oil than black peppercorns, as this is in the skin, so they have less aroma and a sweetish pungency to them.

miscs.name: Potassium Metabisulfite
miscs.notes: Source of SO2 for sanitizing and protecting wine, cider and mead; dose by pH.

miscs.name: Potassium Sorbate
miscs.notes: Stops renewed fermentation before backsweetening; use together with sulfite.

miscs.name: Rooibos
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 52-70 EBC (typical 61) Rooibos, a popular South African herbal tea, has found its way into the world of beer brewing and is making quite an impact. Known for its distinct flavor profile that includes sweet, nutty notes with hints of caramel and vanilla, Rooibos adds complexity and depth to beer. Its unique taste is influencing the overall flavor by providing a malty sweetness that balances out bitterness or hoppy flavors in beers. The properties of Rooibos make it suitable for various applications in brewing. It can be used as an ingredient during mashing or steeped like tea after fermentation to infuse the desired flavors into the final product. Rooibos is often employed in specialty beers such as red ales, Belgian-style witbiers, or even stouts where it complements roasted malt characters exceptionally well. With its versatility and flavorful qualities, Rooibos brings a touch of uniqueness to traditional beer styles while offering brewers endless possibilities for experimentation and creativity. Whether used as an infusion or added directly to the brew kettle, Rooibos provides an exciting twist on familiar beer styles that will surely entice adventurous drinkers seeking something new and delightful.

miscs.name: Saffron
miscs.notes: Saffron is the most expensive spice on Earth. This is because of the labour involved in growing and harvesting the spice. Saffron is the red-yellow stigma of the crocus flower and must be hand-picked during short annual flowering seasons. Each flower produces only three stigmas, so it takes approximately 150 flowers to yield just one gram of dry saffron threads.

miscs.name: Sanaam Chiles
miscs.notes: Sanaam chiles are red and flat, and are 2 to 4 inches in length. They have a medium-high heat.

miscs.name: Star Anise
miscs.notes: Star anise is undisputedly the prettiest spice of them all. Native to China and Vietnam, star anise is the fruit of an evergreen magnolia tree. The fruits are in the shape of an eight-pointed star, and each point holds a shiny brown seed. Star anise has a sweet, licoricey taste, and is used to flavour several liqueurs such as Sambuca, Galliano and pastis.

miscs.name: Sulfuric Acid 10%
miscs.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

miscs.name: Sumac
miscs.notes: Sumac is the berry of a shrub that grows in the Mediterranean and parts of the Middle East. It has a tart, fruity flavour, and is used to add acidity to food.

miscs.name: Table Salt
miscs.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

miscs.name: Tartaric Acid
miscs.notes: The main acid in grapes; used to raise acidity in wine.

miscs.name: Tien Tsin Chiles
miscs.notes: Tien Tsin chiles are very hot Chinese chiles that are particularly suited to Hunan and Szechuan cuisines.

miscs.name: Tonka Beans
miscs.notes: Tonka beans are very unusual little beans that grow primarily in the northern part of South America. They share a lot of similarities with vanilla beans, to the point where they are sometimes used as a vanilla substitute. They are black and wrinkly, about an inch long, and have a sweet flavour that is like a combination of vanilla, cloves and cinnamon with a nuttiness reminiscent of almonds. Really delicious and unusual.

miscs.name: Vanilla
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 2-47 EBC (typical 12) Vanilla, a popular spice and herb, has found its way into the world of beer brewing, adding a delightful twist to various styles. Known for its sweet and creamy flavor profile with hints of caramel and floral undertones, Vanilla brings a unique richness to beers. When used in moderation, it can enhance the complexity and depth of flavors in both dark and light beers. Influencing the taste of beer, Vanilla imparts a smooth sweetness that balances well with different malt profiles. It adds an inviting aroma that complements the overall experience of drinking beer. Vanilla is commonly used as an adjunct ingredient during brewing or added through aging on oak barrels soaked in Vanilla extract or beans. Apart from its delectable taste characteristics, Vanilla possesses certain properties that make it favorable for use in beer production. Its natural oils contribute to improved head retention while lending a velvety mouthfeel to the brews. Additionally, vanillin compounds present in Vanilla act as antioxidants which help preserve the freshness of beers over time. Typical beer styles brewed with Vanilla include stouts, porters, brown ales, cream ales, Belgian quadrupels (Quad), and barleywines. These styles benefit from the addition of Vanilla by creating harmonious flavor combinations such as chocolate- Vanilla notes in stouts or caramel- Vanilla accents in porters.

miscs.name: Whirlfloc Tablet
miscs.notes: Aids in clearing yeast and chill haze. Easy to use tablet form.

miscs.name: Whisky
miscs.notes: Typical color range: 2-47 EBC (typical 3) Whisky, with its distinct flavor profile characterized by smoky, peaty, and caramel notes, has become a popular ingredient in beer brewing. Its influence on the taste of beer adds complexity and depth to the final product. When used in moderation, Whisky can enhance the maltiness of beers by imparting rich flavors that complement the existing ingredients. The application of Whisky in beer brewing is versatile and can be used for various purposes. It can be added during fermentation or aging to infuse unique characteristics into the beer. Whisky also acts as a preservative due to its high alcohol content and contributes to an extended shelf life for certain styles of beers. Properties such as oakiness from barrel aging or hints of vanilla from specific whiskies lend themselves well to certain beer styles. Scotch Ales benefit from the addition of Whisky as it complements their malty sweetness perfectly. Similarly, stouts and porters gain richness when aged in whiskey barrels or infused with whiskey itself.

miscs.name: White Pepper
miscs.notes: White Pepper, a popular spice in Asian cuisine, has also found its way into the world of beer brewing. Known for its pungent and slightly floral flavor profile, White Pepper adds a unique twist to beers by infusing them with hints of earthiness and heat. Its influence on the taste of beer can vary depending on the amount used; a small quantity might provide subtle undertones while larger amounts can create a more pronounced spiciness. White Pepper is typically added during the brewing process as an ingredient to enhance complexity and depth in certain beer styles. It pairs exceptionally well with Belgian-style beers such as saisons or farmhouse ales, where it complements the fruity esters produced by Belgian yeast strains. Additionally, this spice can be incorporated into other beer styles like stouts or wheat beers to introduce an unexpected element that tantalizes the palate. Apart from its distinct flavor characteristics, White Pepper possesses several properties that make it suitable for brewing applications. Firstly, it acts as a natural preservative due to its antimicrobial properties which help prolong shelf life. Furthermore, when used correctly in moderation, it contributes not only aromatic qualities but also aids in achieving balance within the overall flavor profile of the beer.

miscs.name: Wine Tannin
miscs.notes: Adds structure and mouthfeel, especially to fruit wines, cider and mead.

miscs.notes: Helps restart and prevent stuck fermentations.

equipment.name: All Grain - Standard 5 Gal/19l Batch - Cooler
equipment.notes: Popular all grain setup. 5 Gal/19 l Plastic cooler as mash tun with false bottom, and 7-9 gallon brewpot capable of boiling at least 7 gal of wort without spilling over. Primarily used for single infusion mashes.
equipment.source_names: Canadian Homebrewers Association via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Anvil Foundry 10.5 gal
equipment.notes: Batches ~5 gal. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 0.4 gal, boil-off 1 gal/h at 240 V (less at 120 V).
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Anvil Foundry 18 gal
equipment.notes: Batches 5-10 gal. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 0.6 gal, boil-off 1.25 gal/h. Mash: Up to 36 lb grain.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Anvil Foundry 6.5 gal
equipment.notes: Batches 2.5-3 gal. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 0.25 gal, boil-off 0.75 gal/h at 240 V (less at 120 V).
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brew Monk B40
equipment.notes: 40 L total; batch 10-30 L. Weight 13 kg (Brouwland listing). Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 1.5 L, boil-off 3.5 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe takes up to 8 kg.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brew Monk B50
equipment.notes: 52 L total; batch 15-40 L. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 2 L, boil-off 4 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe takes up to 12 kg.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brew Monk B70
equipment.notes: 70 L total; batch 25-65 L. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 3 L, boil-off 4 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe takes up to 18 kg. default_batch_size is 63 L rather than the manufacturer's 65 L, as 65 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (4 L) and kettle loss (3 L) would not fit in the 70 L kettle.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewferm Beer Brew 25
equipment.notes: 34 L gross capacity; up to 25 L wort. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 1.5 L, boil-off 3 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe 21 L. (Older model, now hard to find new.)
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewferm Brewer 30 L
equipment.notes: 30 L total, 25 L to the max line; ~20 L batches. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 1.5 L, boil-off 3 L/h. Mash: Unlike the other systems in this file, there is no malt pipe or pump: the Brewer is an electric kettle with thermostat, used brew-in-a-bag (Brewferm sells a false bottom for this). The drained wort stays in the kettle; grain absorption is lower (~0.66 L/kg) if you squeeze the bag.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewster Beacon 40
equipment.notes: 40 L total; batch 12.5-30 L. Weight 10 kg; Ø 36 cm (outside). Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 1.5 L, boil-off 3.5 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe takes up to 9 kg.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewster Beacon 70
equipment.notes: 70 L total; batch 25-65 L. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 3 L, boil-off 4 L/h, Ø ~40 cm (from 40.5 cm outside dimension). Mash: Malt pipe takes up to 18 kg. default_batch_size is 63 L rather than the manufacturer's 65 L, as 65 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (4 L) and kettle loss (3 L) would not fit in the 70 L kettle.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewtools B150pro
equipment.notes: Tank 170 L; pre-boil up to ~150 L. Weight 37.6 kg; tank Ø 60 cm. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 5 L, boil-off 7 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe Ø 50 cm, up to 35 kg grain; minimum ~35 L liquid in the tank.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewtools B40pro
equipment.notes: Tank ~46 L; pre-boil 20-40 L. Weight 20 kg; tank Ø 40 cm. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 1.5 L, boil-off 3.5 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe 25.7 L (Ø 32 cm), up to ~9 kg grain; minimum ~15 L liquid in the tank. Conical, centre-drained bottom.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewtools B50
equipment.notes: New model (US availability announced for January 2027). Total capacity 52 L; batch 10-40 L; tank Ø 40 cm. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 2 L, boil-off 4 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe Ø 31.5 cm, up to 10 kg grain.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Brewtools B80pro
equipment.notes: Tank 90 L; pre-boil 30-80 L. Weight 27 kg; tank Ø 50 cm. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 3 L, boil-off 6 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe Ø 42 cm, up to 20 kg grain; minimum ~25 L liquid in the tank.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: BrewZilla 100 L (Gen 4)
equipment.notes: Max 100 L (107 L brimful); batches up to ~90 L. Dry weight ~20 kg; ~52 cm outside diameter. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 4 L, boil-off 8 L/h. Mash: Malt pipe 72 L, up to 25 kg grain (20-23 kg typical); minimum 20 L liquid in the boiler. default_batch_size is 88 L rather than the manufacturer's 90 L, as 90 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (8 L) and kettle loss (4 L) would not fit in the 100 L kettle.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: BrewZilla 35 L (Gen 4)
equipment.notes: Max 35 L; batches up to ~25 L. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 1.5 L, boil-off 3 L/h. Mash: Up to 11.5 kg grain (4-5 kg typical); minimum 4 L liquid in the boiler. False bottom sits ~14 mm above the base.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: BrewZilla 65 L (Gen 4)
equipment.notes: Max 65 L; batches up to ~50-55 L. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 2.5 L, boil-off 5 L/h. Mash: foundation_volume is KegLand's figure for the space below the false bottom. Up to 18.5 kg grain (10-14 kg typical); minimum 4 L liquid in the boiler.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Grainfather G30 (v3)
equipment.notes: Max pre-boil 30 L; batch 10-25 L. Loss (2 L, trub + chiller) and boil-off (3 L/h at 230 V, ~2 L/h at 120 V) are Grainfather's own example figures. Mash: foundation_volume is Grainfather's figure for the space below the basket. Grain bill 1.5-8 kg (9 kg with top plate extension). Grainfather uses 0.8 L/kg grain absorption and 2.7 L/kg mash thickness.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Grainfather G40
equipment.notes: Max pre-boil 46 L; batch 10-40 L. Weight 29 kg empty. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 2.5 L, boil-off 4 L/h, internal diameter ~53 cm (from 555 mm overall width). Mash: Dished centre drain means essentially no volume below the plate (per Grainfather), hence foundation_volume of 0. Grain bill 3-13 kg. default_batch_size is 39.5 L rather than the manufacturer's 40 L, as 40 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (4 L) and kettle loss (2.5 L) would not fit in the 46 L kettle.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Grainfather G70 (v2)
equipment.notes: Max pre-boil 60 L; batch 30-58 L. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 3 L, boil-off 4.5 L/h, internal diameter ~53 cm (from 555 mm overall width). Mash: foundation_volume is Grainfather's figure for the space below the basket. Grain bill 8-16 kg (17 kg with top plate extension). default_batch_size is 52.5 L rather than the manufacturer's 58 L, as 58 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (4.5 L) and kettle loss (3 L) would not fit in the 60 L kettle.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Speidel Braumeister 100 L
equipment.notes: Nominal 100 L. Weight 77 kg. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: max volume 110 L (by analogy with the smaller models), loss 5 L, boil-off 6 L/h. Mash: Max 21 kg malt. default_batch_size is 99 L rather than the manufacturer's 100 L, as 100 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (6 L) and kettle loss (5 L) would not fit in the 110 L kettle.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Speidel Braumeister 1000 L
equipment.notes: Nominal 1000 L. Weight 850 kg. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: max volume 1100 L, loss 40 L, boil-off 35 L/h. Mash: Max 225 kg malt.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Speidel Braumeister 200 L
equipment.notes: Nominal 200 L. Weight 150 kg. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: max volume 220 L, loss 10 L, boil-off 9 L/h. Mash: Max 42 kg malt.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Speidel Braumeister 500 L
equipment.notes: Nominal 500 L. Weight 380 kg. Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: max volume 550 L, loss 20 L, boil-off 18 L/h. Mash: Max 120 kg malt.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Speidel Braumeister PLUS 10 L
equipment.notes: Max fill 12 L; ~11 L wort, ~10 L finished beer. Weight 12 kg; diameter 30 cm (outside). Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 0.5 L, boil-off 1 L/h. Mash: Max 2.8 kg malt; 12 L water filled for mashing, 15-20 L brewing water per batch. default_batch_size is 10.5 L rather than the manufacturer's 11 L, as 11 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (1 L) and kettle loss (0.5 L) would not fit in the 12 L kettle.
equipment.source_names: DotBeer example library via Brewtarget DefaultContent005

equipment.name: Speidel Braumeister PLUS 20 L
equipment.notes: Max fill 25 L; ~23 L wort, ~20 L finished beer. Weight 19 kg; diameter 40 cm (outside). Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 1.5 L, boil-off 2 L/h. Mash: Max 6 kg malt; 23 L water filled for mashing, 25-30 L brewing water per batch. default_batch_size is 21.5 L rather than the manufacturer's 23 L, as 23 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (2 L) and kettle loss (1.5 L) would not fit in the 25 L kettle.

equipment.name: Speidel Braumeister PLUS 50 L
equipment.notes: Max fill 55 L; ~53 L wort, ~50 L finished beer. Weight 24 kg (manual; Speidel's comparison page says 30 kg); diameter 50 cm (outside). Estimated (no manufacturer figure) -- calibrate on your own system: loss 2.5 L, boil-off 3 L/h. Mash: Max 13 kg malt; 55 L water filled for mashing, 55-60 L brewing water per batch. default_batch_size is 49.5 L rather than the manufacturer's 53 L, as 53 L plus a 60 minute boil-off (3 L) and kettle loss (2.5 L) would not fit in the 55 L kettle.
